paragraphs.source_en: “Next, turning to England, we find in Beowulf the word for gallows, namely galga, and so I believe the punishment of hanging must have begun in that age. According to Blackstone, if a person sentenced to hanging should, by some mishap of the rope, fail to die, he is to undergo the same punishment a second time. Strangely enough, however, in Piers Plowman there is a line saying that even a villain ought not to be hanged twice. Well, I shall not go into which account is correct. Still, there was indeed an actual case in which a man could not be killed by hanging. In 1786, a notorious villain named Fitz-Gerald was hanged. By some curious accident, the rope broke the first time he jumped from the platform. They tried again; this time the rope was too long, his feet touched the ground, and once more he failed to die, so at last they attempted it a third time. It is said that this time, with the help of the spectators, they finally sent him to the next world.”
